verses.text: At that time Abijah the son of Jeroboam became sick.

Jeroboam said to his wife, “Please get up and disguise yourself, so that you won’t be recognized as Jeroboam’s wife. Go to Shiloh. Behold, Ahijah the prophet is there, who said that that I would be king over this people.
Take with you ten loaves of bread, some cakes, and a jar of honey, and go to him. He will tell you what will become of the child.”
Jeroboam’s wife did so, and arose, and went to Shiloh, and came to Ahijah’s house. Now Ahijah could not see; for his eyes were set by reason of his age.

Yahweh said to Ahijah, “Behold, Jeroboam’s wife is coming to inquire of you concerning her son; for he is sick. Tell her such and such; for it will be, when she comes in, that she will pretend to be another woman.”
So when Ahijah heard the sound of her feet as she came in at the door, he said, “Come in, Jeroboam’s wife! Why do you pretend to be another? For I am sent to you with heavy news.
Go, tell Jeroboam, ‘Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: “Because I exalted you from among the people, and made you prince over my people Israel,

and tore the kingdom away from David’s house, and gave it you; and yet you have not been as my servant David, who kept my commandments, and who followed me with all his heart, to do that only which was right in my eyes,
but have done evil above all who were before you, and have gone and made for yourself other gods, molten images, to provoke me to anger, and have cast me behind your back;

therefore, behold, I will bring evil on the house of Jeroboam, and will cut off from Jeroboam everyone who urinates on a wall,  he who is shut up and he who is left at large in Israel, and will utterly sweep away the house of Jeroboam, as a man sweeps away dung, until it is all gone.
The dogs will eat he who belongs to Jeroboam who dies in the city; and the birds of the sky will eat he who dies in the field: for Yahweh has spoken it.”’
Arise therefore, and go to your house. When your feet enter into the city, the child will die.
All Israel will mourn for him and bury him; for he only of Jeroboam will come to the grave, because in him there is found some good thing toward Yahweh, the God of Israel, in the house of Jeroboam.
Moreover Yahweh will raise up a king for himself over Israel, who will cut off the house of Jeroboam. This is the day! What? Even now.

For Yahweh will strike Israel, as a reed is shaken in the water; and he will root up Israel out of this good land which he gave to their fathers, and will scatter them beyond the River,  because they have made their Asherah poles, provoking Yahweh to anger.
He will give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam, which he has sinned, and with which he has made Israel to sin.”
Jeroboam’s wife arose and departed, and came to Tirzah. As she came to the threshold of the house, the child died.
All Israel buried him and mourned for him, according to Yahweh’s word, which he spoke by his servant Ahijah the prophet.
The rest of the acts of Jeroboam, how he fought, and how he reigned, behold, they are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
The days which Jeroboam reigned were twenty two years, then he slept with his fathers, and Nadab his son reigned in his place.

Rehoboam the son of Solomon reigned in Judah. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city which Yahweh had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, to put his name there. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonitess.
Judah did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, and they provoked him to jealousy with their sins which they committed, above all that their fathers had done.
For they also built for themselves high places, sacred pillars, and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every green tree.
There were also sodomites in the land. They did according to all the abominations of the nations which Yahweh drove out before the children of Israel.
In the fifth year of king Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem,
and he took away the treasures of Yahweh’s house, and the treasures of the king’s house. He even took away all of it, including all the gold shields which Solomon had made.
King Rehoboam made shields of brass in their place, and committed them to the hands of the captains of the guard, who kept the door of the king’s house.
It was so, that as often as the king went into Yahweh’s house, the guard bore them, and brought them back into the guard room.
Now the rest of the acts of Rehoboam, and all that he did, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually.
Rehoboam slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in David’s city. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonitess. Abijam his son reigned in his place.

footnotes.content: A child falls ill, and a king's heart runs to shadow-seeking. Jeroboam moves fast to consult Ahijah—the same prophet who once spoke his rise—hoping for rescue through back channels. It's the old reach-for-human-wisdom before the soul can rest in God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wife's disguise cuts me. Jeroboam sends her to Shiloh with false identity, as if the Lord could be fooled by a borrowed cloak. Sometimes we think covering our tracks shows wisdom, when the Lord sees clear through to the naked heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A jar of honey, bread, cakes—gifts meant to sweeten the prophet's tongue. Yet what good are offerings if we come in disguise? The Lord doesn't need our tribute; He asks for truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahijah is old and blind—his eyes 'set by reason of age.' Here walks a man who has watched kingdoms rise and stumble. Yet he sees what none of Jeroboam's eyes can see: the end already written.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord Himself tells Ahijah what will unfold—not as mere guessing, but as sovereign knowledge. She will enter in pretense; the word will fall hard and true. God does not require our clever masks to know us and speak rightly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahijah hears her footstep and speaks her name: 'Come in, Jeroboam's wife!' The disguise crumbles the moment she crosses the threshold. And his word: 'Heavy news'—a prophet's kindness even as the truth comes hard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh reminds Jeroboam of his own beginning—plucked from nothing, made prince. The whole grace-history laid bare before judgment. We forget so easily what the Lord has done, how He reached and lifted us up.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David stands here as the measure—'he kept my commandments and followed me with all his heart.' Not a perfect king, yet a king who turned again and again toward his Maker, who loved with devotion. That's the comparison; that's the weight Jeroboam could not bear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam has done worse than those before him—and he made others sin alongside him. When we lead, we lead downward or upward; there is no neutral. He fashioned idols with his own hands and taught the people to worship them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The language is brutal—no one will be left standing, not even memory will remain unswept. It reminds us that faithlessness does not die quietly; it empties a house entirely. Mercy was offered at the start. Now comes the end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Dogs and birds will scatter what remains—no burial honor, no grave. It sounds harsh until we remember that Jeroboam chose to sow contempt toward God. Reaping what he sowed is not cruelty; it is just measure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A threshold crossed, and it's done. Before her foot touches her own city, the child is gone. Mercy comes as swift judgment—the boy will have no long sickness, no drawn-out suffering. Sometimes the kindest word is brief.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the boy, 'some good thing toward Yahweh' is found. Only he of Jeroboam's line will rest in a grave—the others will be scattered, but this child goes whole to the fathers. One small good found in a bent house; the Lord sees it and honors even that.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'This is the day! What? Even now'—the prophet's words break with the urgency of it. Not someday, but today. Not a distant future, but the moment itself. When judgment comes, it comes quickly, and we are caught.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel shaken like a reed, then uprooted entirely. The 'good land' their fathers received will no longer hold them. When a people turn from God, even the land rises up against them. It is not that God loves less; it is that He loves truthfully, and truth has edges.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam's sin reaches downward—he has 'made Israel to sin.' A leader's unfaith becomes the nation's trap. What one man plants in stone the people reap for generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She rises and departs, her errand done. The words spoken cannot be unspoken. She arrives home to Tirzah, her foot crosses the threshold, and the thing is finished—the child already gone. Prophecy and reality meet at the threshold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All Israel buries the boy and mourns. Even in judgment, there is a grave and honor. The nation sees the Lord's word proven true through the prophet's mouth. Fear and respect mingle in that burial.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeroboam's deeds are written in the chronicles—wars, reign, all recorded. Yet no record saves a faithless king from judgment. History remembers; God judges. The two are not the same.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twenty-two years he reigned, then 'slept with his fathers.' Even a king must lay down his crown at last. Nadab inherits—another chance for the line, another chapter. The throne does not wait for us; it only turns.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rehoboam, son of Solomon—named by choice, not accident. Forty-one when he took the throne; seventeen years he held Judah. Jerusalem, the city of God's choosing, lay in his care. How much weight does one man carry?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah 'did that which was evil' and provoked Yahweh to jealousy. To provoke God is to treat His love as though it were a thing to toy with. But God's jealousy is not petty—it guards the covenant, the belonging He offers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: High places, sacred pillars, Asherah poles—they built altars everywhere, as if covering the land with idols made God more real. Yet every shrine they raised was a denial of the one God. When we multiply false gods, we deny the true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the abominations of the nations—practices the Lord had driven out—now flourish in Judah. To adopt the ways of those God cast down is to align yourself with the cast-down. The people chose the company of the expelled.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the fifth year—precisely marked—Shishak of Egypt comes up against Jerusalem. The timing is no accident; judgment through human hands often wears an earthly face. Pharaoh moves, yet the Lord's purpose is written in the move.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The treasures are taken—Yahweh's own house ransacked, the gold shields of Solomon melted down. Solomon had gathered such riches; now they flow into another's hands. Wealth gathers and scatters; only faithfulness holds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rehoboam makes shields of brass—a substitute, a lesser thing. When we lose the true, we often patch with the false, telling ourselves it will do. Brass is not gold, but we walk on with what remains.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The guard carries the brass shields in and out each time the king enters Yahweh's house—a ritual of substitution, a public sign of loss. Yet the Lord's house still stands, and worship continues, even if in diminished glory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Aren't they written in the book of the chronicles?' The refrain reminds us that human deeds are recorded, yet the record alone does not redeem them. History keeps accounts; only God judges justly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: War between Rehoboam and Jeroboam 'continually'—a kingdom divided cannot hold. Readers today hear an echo: whenever Christ's people fracture over pride or doctrine, we weaken and invite the world's contempt. The unity the Lord wills is not mere niceness; it's strength.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rehoboam sleeps with his fathers and is buried in David's city. The line continues—Abijam takes the throne next. Kings pass; the kingdom endures. Yet the question lingers: will the son turn his face back toward the Lord?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
